content: Nevus depigmentosus, also known as nevus achromicus, is a condition characterized by areas of hypopigmentation on the skin. These hypopigmented patches are distinct from vitiligo and are typically present at birth in approximately 19% of cases. While the size of the patches may increase proportionally with the growth of the body, their distribution remains stable, and the condition is nonprogressive. Individuals with nevus depigmentosus are at an increased risk of sunburn due to the lack of protective pigment in the affected areas. Therefore, it is essential to use adequate sun protection, including the application of sunscreen to all exposed skin. This not only prevents sunburn but also minimizes the contrast between hypopigmented and normal skin by reducing tanning of unaffected areas. Most patients with nevus depigmentosus do not seek treatment for their lesions, as there is currently no method to restore pigmentation to the affected areas. For those who are concerned about the cosmetic appearance of the lesions, camouflage makeup can be an effective option. In cases where the lesion is small, surgical excision may be considered. The exact etiology of nevus depigmentosus remains unclear. It is hypothesized to result from a sporadic defect during embryonic development. Although it has been described as localized albinism, this terminology is inaccurate. The hypopigmented patches are caused by functional abnormalities in melanocytes, the cells responsible for producing pigment. These melanocytes produce significantly reduced amounts of pigment, leading to the characteristic white spots on the skin. Nevus depigmentosus must be differentiated from vitiligo during diagnosis. On physical examination, the condition presents as localized white spots that can occur on any part of the body. These lesions are stable and do not progress over time. Most lesions are not completely devoid of pigment but are hypopigmented, often resembling splashed paint. If hair is present in the affected area, it is typically colorless or white. The lesions are permanent and do not resolve spontaneously. There are no effective treatments available to repigment the affected areas in nevus depigmentosus. Various therapeutic approaches have been attempted, including PUVA therapy (psoralen combined with UVA light), excimer laser treatment, and grafting techniques. However, PUVA therapy has not demonstrated any significant benefit. A single case of successful repigmentation was reported following 14 sessions of excimer laser treatment, but such outcomes are rare. Grafting techniques may achieve repigmentation in some cases, but the results are inconsistent, and recurrence of hypopigmentation is possible. The quality and durability of the pigment achieved through these methods are unpredictable. These factors should be carefully considered when discussing treatment options with patients.
